criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Identifies several ethical issues (test coverage by schedule, data-loss/harm link, conflict of interest), explicitly frames them as organisational design-process decisions, and provides a detailed stakeholder table with interests and decision control.

evidence.quote: Three ethical issues follow. First, test coverage is being set by the release calendar instead of by risk
Table 1 summarises who they are, what each has at stake and what each can decide.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Objective, evidence-based arguments for and against shipping with significant depth; conclusions include decision-making recommendations for Rachel, management, health department, chip supplier and engineers — multiple stakeholders covered.

evidence.quote: Shipping on time protects a real competitive advantage. Stalk showed that firms which shorten their development cycles
separate recommendations for her company, the health department and the chip supplier.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Logically ordered body: for-arguments then their systematic rebuttal, a decision rule (Figure 1), option trade-off table, and a conclusion directly derived from the arguments. Systematic understanding across all stakeholders is evident.

evidence.quote: Options B and C respect every stakeholder's interests better than either extreme.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Eight reputable references (NAO, Leveson & Turner, Intel annual report, DOJ, Standards Australia, EA Code, HBR). Both quantitative evidence (81/236 trusts, 19,000 appointments, US$475M, US$4.3B) and qualitative case analysis; balanced treatment including caveats (e.g., WannaCry cause distinction).

evidence.quote: an estimated 19,000 appointments were cancelled and patients in five areas were diverted
[3] National Audit Office, "Investigation: WannaCry cyber attack and the NHS"

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: Fluent, concise writing; IEEE-style references consistently formatted; a figure and two tables used competently. Minor deductions: inconsistent heading levels (####/#####/###), abstract slightly over ~150 words, only one figure type. Still very good rather than flawless.

technical_issues.issue: Abstract is ~170 words, slightly above the ~150-word target.
WannaCry case involves ransomware, not hardware defects; student acknowledges this limitation appropriately, so not a substantive flaw.

overall: An outstanding, well-researched ethics report. Ethical issues, organisational context and stakeholders are thoroughly identified; arguments are balanced, evidence-based and quantitatively supported; the decision rule, option table and multi-stakeholder recommendations flow logically to a justified conclusion. Only minor formatting and abstract-length issues prevent a perfect structure mark.

feedback.summary: An outstanding, well-researched ethics report. You thoroughly identified the ethical issues, organisational context and stakeholders, and built balanced, evidence-based arguments with quantitative support. Your decision rule, option table and multi-stakeholder recommendations flow logically to a justified conclusion. Only minor formatting and abstract-length issues prevented a perfect structure mark.
next_steps: Trim the abstract to the ~150-word target; it currently runs to about 170 words.
Standardise heading levels throughout (you mix ####/#####/### inconsistently) and check they follow your template's hierarchy.
Add one or two more visual element types (e.g., a stakeholder influence map or timeline) to complement Figure 1 and Tables 1–2.

criteria.C1: Excellent work. You identified several ethical issues (test coverage driven by schedule, data-loss/harm, conflict of interest), framed them as organisational design-process decisions, and your Table 1 clearly mapped stakeholders, their stakes and decision control. To sustain this level, keep explicitly linking each new issue back to both organisational context and stakeholder interests as you did here.
criteria.C2: Excellent. Your arguments for and against shipping were objective, evidence-based and appropriately deep, and your recommendations addressed Rachel, management, the health department, the chip supplier and engineers. Maintain this breadth by always asking which stakeholders a conclusion serves, as your RECOMMENDATIONS section successfully did.
criteria.C3: Excellent. The body's structure — for-arguments, systematic rebuttals, the Figure 1 decision rule, and the Table 2 trade-off analysis — built compellingly to your conclusion that Options B and C best respect all stakeholders. Keep using this pattern of argument-then-rebuttal to make future conclusions equally well supported.
criteria.C4: Excellent research. Eight reputable references (NAO, Leveson & Turner, Intel, DOJ, Standards Australia, EA Code, HBR) combined quantitative evidence (81/236 trusts, 19,000 cancelled appointments, US$475M, US$4.3B) with qualitative case analysis, and you appropriately caveated the WannaCry cause distinction. Continue balancing both evidence types in future work.
criteria.C5: Very good. Your writing is fluent and concise, IEEE references are consistently formatted, and Figure 1 and Tables 1–2 are used competently. To reach the excellent level: fix the inconsistent heading levels, tighten the abstract to ~150 words, and incorporate a wider variety of visual elements.
